heading: Background
html: The common presentations are lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow), medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow), olecranon bursitis and cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve compression at the elbow). Around 90% of epicondylitis settles within a year with conservative management. True elbow joint arthritis is uncommon and usually post-traumatic or inflammatory.

heading: Assessment
html:
• Lateral epicondylitis: pain over lateral epicondyle, worse on resisted wrist/finger extension and gripping.
  • Medial epicondylitis: pain over medial epicondyle, worse on resisted wrist flexion/pronation.
  • Olecranon bursitis: fluctuant swelling over the olecranon; joint movement typically preserved (unlike septic arthritis).
  • Cubital tunnel: tingling/numbness of ring and little fingers, worse with prolonged elbow flexion (phone use, sleeping); check for weakness of grip/pinch and first dorsal interosseous or hypothenar wasting.
  • Locking or true mechanical block suggests loose bodies or joint pathology — examine for fixed flexion and X-ray.

Red flags — same-day discussion

  • Hot, red elbow or bursa with fever or systemic upset (septic bursitis / septic arthritis — see hot swollen joint pathway)
  • Significant trauma with deformity or inability to move the elbow
  • Rapidly progressive neurological deficit

heading: Primary care management
html:
Epicondylitis (lateral and medial):

  • Explain the natural history — most settle within 12 months; this alone reduces re-attendance.
  • Modify load (grip size, lifting technique, workstation); relative rest, not immobilisation.
  • Progressive loading exercises — self-directed (NHS Inform) or physiotherapy via Single Access Point (030 3333 3001).
  • Analgesia: topical NSAID (e.g. topical Ibuprofen) or short course of oral NSAID.
  • Counterforce brace/strap may help symptoms during activity.
  • Avoid corticosteroid injection — short-term relief but worse outcomes at 6–12 months and higher recurrence.

Olecranon bursitis (non-septic): avoid pressure/leaning, NSAIDs, compression; aspiration only if diagnostic doubt — recurrence after aspiration is common. Do not inject steroid routinely (infection and skin atrophy risk).

Cubital tunnel: avoid prolonged/repetitive elbow flexion and direct pressure; night extension positioning (towel splint); review at 6–12 weeks.

heading: Who to refer
html:
Same day

  • Suspected septic bursitis or septic arthritis (hot, red, fever) — discuss with orthopaedics on call
  • Acute trauma with suspected fracture/dislocation — ED

Urgent (SCI Gateway)

  • Cubital tunnel with motor weakness or muscle wasting — refer with nerve conduction studies requested; delay risks permanent deficit

Routine

  • Epicondylitis with significant symptoms despite 6–12 months of conservative management including a completed loading programme
  • Cubital tunnel with persistent sensory symptoms despite 3 months of conservative management
  • Mechanical locking / loose bodies on X-ray
  • Recurrent troublesome bursitis

Include in referral: duration, conservative measures tried (and for how long), occupational demands, neurological findings, and X-ray/NCS results where done.

heading: Who not to refer
html:
• Epicondylitis of less than 6 months' duration without a completed conservative programme — most will settle.
  • Simple non-septic olecranon bursitis — manage conservatively.
  • Cubital tunnel with intermittent positional symptoms only, improving with positioning advice.
  • Asymptomatic radiographic changes.
